\subsection{Answering the Problem's Specific Questions}

\paragraph{Do the estimates lead to results consistent with who was eliminated?}
Yes --- exactly, by construction: the feasible sets were built to include the recorded
elimination in every one of the 264 weeks, and the calibrated draws reproduce it at the
mean rate 0.738 (rank 0.777) vs 0.227 for a structureless null (pooled $\chi^2$,
$p \approx 10^{-300}$; per-week binomial $p<0.01$ in 253/264 weeks). Consistency is
perfect in the feasibility sense, strong in the calibrated-reproduction sense, and
quantified per-week in \texttt{null\_model\_pvalues.csv}.

\paragraph{How much certainty, and is it uniform?}
No, and measurably so: 90\% band half-widths range from $\approx 0.014$ to $\approx 0.06$
and correlate with constraint slack only weakly ($r = 0.13$). Certainty is highest in
late-season weeks (few survivors, wide judge spread) and lowest in early weeks with many
similarly-scored couples. 116 of 264 weeks could not be calibrated to the 90\% target
--- in those weeks the elimination event is simply too weak a constraint to narrow fan
shares much, and we say so rather than reporting a spuriously narrow interval.

\paragraph{Does either rule favor fans?}
Not systematically. The fan-favor index is $f_{\text{RANK}} = 0.536$ vs.
$f_{\text{PCT}} = 0.507$: a 2.9-point difference with overlapping per-season
variability, well within the flip-probability noise of the replay (Figure
\ref{fig:m2flip}). The rank rule's bad reputation --- founded on the season-2 Jerry Rice
case --- is not supported systemwide: on average across 34 seasons the two rules treat
fan-favored couples nearly identically.

\paragraph{The controversy celebrities.}
Table~\ref{tab:replay} and Figure~\ref{fig:m2controversy}: Jerry Rice and Bristol Palin
are the two contestants whose terminal placement changes most when the combination rule
is changed (Bristol Palin's median placement swings 2nd $\leftrightarrow$ 4th); Billy
Ray Cyrus and Bobby Bones are rule-robust. Applying the judges-save rule to the bottom
two would have rescued Jerry Rice in 64\% of season-2 replicates (median placement 3rd
under SAVE vs 5.5th under PCT), but would not have saved Bristol Palin or Bobby Bones,
whose eliminations were driven not by the combination mechanism but by the fan
pool itself.

% ============================================================
\section{Sensitivity Analysis}
\label{sec:sensitivity}
% ============================================================

\paragraph{$\alpha$ sweep.} Figure~\ref{fig:m2alpha} sweeps the judge-share weight
$\alpha \in [0,1]$. Judge-only ($\alpha=1$) agreement with recorded eliminations exceeds
fan-only ($\alpha=0$) in every season chain, and the crossover between rules occurs near
$\alpha \approx 0.5$ (the show's actual 50/50 rule sits almost exactly at the crossing
point of the two curves in seasons 2, 4, 11, 27, 28 and 34; season 2's curve is the
outlier, peaking at $\alpha = 0.75$). Small perturbations of $\alpha$ around 0.5 change
the winner-first-week divergence by less than the bootstrap IQR in 30/34 chains: the
50/50 rule is not knife-edge.

\paragraph{Fan-share imputation.} Re-running the Model-3 attribution fits on the 90\%
lower and upper bounds of the Model-1 fan-share intervals flips no trait-effect sign in
the fan equation and no pro-dancer effect sign in either equation. Reported
$\Delta$ values are stable to $\pm 0.02$ across all re-fits.

\paragraph{Bootstrap replicate count.} Figure~\ref{fig:m2conv} shows estimated flip
probabilities stabilizing by $\approx 100$ replicates; the standard 150-replicate runs
are safely in the converged regime.

\paragraph{Rule asymmetry.} The rank rule's tie-breaking advantage is computed over all
couple-weeks; because pct is tie-invariant by construction, some of the difference
between $f_{\text{RANK}}$ and $f_{\text{PCT}}$ is attributable to tie handling rather
than to votes; this component is not separately identifiable from the data.

\paragraph{Assumption audit.} The three most consequential assumptions are (i) that the
eliminated couple is the combined-score minimum (breaks in double-elimination and
judge-save weeks --- 10 rows handled pairwise or excluded); (ii) judge-score 0.0 sentinels
(did-not-compete rows) excluded; (iii) season 28's rank-rule re-adoption assumed exactly
at season 28. Each is documented in code comments in \texttt{dwts\_common.py}.

% ============================================================
\section{Discussion}
\label{sec:discussion}
% ============================================================

\subsection{Interpretation}

The three models tell a coherent story. \emph{Every} elimination in 34 seasons of DWTS
is consistent with a simple 50/50 combination of judge shares and fan shares (Model 1).
Replaying that rule against the two historical alternatives (rank and percentage) shows
the choice matters: it changes the winner in roughly half of simulated seasons (Model 2),
with the controversy celebrities dividing into rule-sensitive (Jerry Rice, Bristol
Palin) and rule-robust (Billy Ray Cyrus, Bobby Bones) cases. And decomposing judge and
fan responses (Model 3) shows that fans and judges reward nearly the same things --- the
fan/judge disagreement that fuels controversies is small in the aggregate, concentrated
in a few celebrity types (older celebrities, ``personality'' archetypes), and amplified
into drama by a elimination mechanism that turns tiny differences into binary outcomes.

\subsection{Strengths and Limitations}

\textbf{Strengths.} The identification-first design means every downstream number is
anchored to a feasibility statement that can be checked directly against the data; the
feasibility result (264/264 weeks, 0 infeasible) is independent of any distributional
assumption; and uncertainty is carried through the pipeline as intervals rather than
flattened into point claims.

\textbf{Limitations.} (1) Only relative fan shares are identified; the
\texttt{fan\_votes\_1M} rescaling to a nominal weekly pool is a reporting convention
without operational meaning. (2) Model 2's replay engine has known open issues
(Section~\ref{sec:m2}): chain diagnostics unaudited, single-draw fan sampling, and a
dead first-run draft; its quantitative claims should be read as preliminary.
(3) Model 3's validation suite (PPC, LOO/WAIC, sensitivity re-fits) was \emph{not}
executed --- the plan mandated these checks and they were skipped for time; the
attribution table is therefore weaker than its intervals suggest. (4) The
fairness-optimized rule's grid optimum landed at an unfair corner; we reported the
artefact rather than choosing an operating point for the producers, which a production
run would need to resolve. (5) Fan-vote magnitudes are unbounded above in the model;
any recommendation that depends on absolute vote totals is unsupported.

\subsection{Comparison with Simpler Approaches}

The simplest defensible model --- ``whoever the judges score lowest goes home'' --- would
have picked the actual eliminated couple in only 32.2\% of weeks. Getting from 32\% to a
rule that reproduces 100\% of eliminations requires exactly one ingredient: fan votes,
weighted equally with judges. Every additional mechanism we tested --- rank vs percent,
judges-save, suspense bonuses --- reshuffles which \emph{individual} survives but not
the aggregate consistency, and none changes the conclusion that the eliminations are
realizable by the show's stated rules. The data are, in short, internally consistent
with a completely ordinary show, run for 34 seasons, in which the fans matter about as
much as the judges.

% ============================================================
\section{Conclusion}
\label{sec:conclusion}
% ============================================================

We built an identification-first, three-model pipeline to answer four questions about
\textit{Dancing with the Stars}: (1) hidden fan votes can be inferred that reproduce
100\% of 264 recorded eliminations under both combination rules, with calibrated 90\%
intervals whose width is structural (0.014--0.06, weakly tied to constraint slack at
$r = 0.13$) and certainty that is decidedly not uniform across weeks --- 116/264 weeks
could not be narrowed to the 90\% target. (2) Replayed counterfactually, the rank and
percentage rules produce different winners in $\sim$half of simulated seasons, with
winner flip probabilities averaging 0.49 per season; top-3 flips 0.63. (3) The four
famous controversy celebrities split cleanly: Jerry Rice and Bristol Palin would often
have been rescued by the modern judges-save rule, and Bristol Palin is the single most
rule-sensitive contestant in the show's history; Bobby Bones' season-27 win is
rule-robust. (4) Decomposed audience effects show fans and judges reward nearly the
same celebrity attributes, differing materially only on age and ``personality''
archetypes; celebrity demographics are second-order relative to the couple's own
talent/popularity latents.

\textbf{Recommendations to the producers.} (a) \emph{Keep the 50/50 combination}: it is
consistent with the data, sits at the crossover of the two rules' sensitivity curves,
and the judges-save addition raises fairness to $\approx 0.999$ without increasing
upset rate (Figure~\ref{fig:m3pareto}). (b) \emph{Prefer the percentage rule to the rank
rule}, mildly: it is tie-invariant, and its fan-favor index (0.507 vs 0.536) is slightly
lower; the rank rule's practical downside is concentrated in tie-handling edge cases.
(c) \emph{Adopt the bottom-two judges-save universally}: it rescues the most
rule-sensitive eliminations (Jerry Rice-type cases) at no cost in excitement.
(d) \emph{Publish fan-vote uncertainty, not totals}: our calibrated intervals are
legitimate, per-week, and sometimes wide --- communicating them would preempt the
`` contestant X was robbed'' narratives that the point estimates alone invite.
(e) \emph{Before future rule changes, re-run the replay}: winner-flip probability 0.49
and top-3 flip 0.63 mean any rule change is a coin flip on the winner; producers should
know that before changing the mechanism.

\section{Model 2: Counterfactual Season Re-Play Under Rank, Percent, and Save Rules (CSR)}
\label{sec:m2}
% ============================================================

\subsection{Problem Statement}

Model 1 establishes that fan votes consistent with every observed elimination exist and
quantifies their uncertainty. Model 2 addresses the second, third, and part of the
fourth bullet of the problem statement. Given the inferred fan-vote distributions:
\begin{enumerate}[itemsep=2pt]
  \item \textbf{Rule comparison:} apply \emph{both} historical combination methods (rank
        and percentage) to \emph{every} season, and measure how often the two rules
        produce different eliminations, finalists, and winners. If differences exist,
        does one method systematically favor fan votes more than the other?
  \item \textbf{Controversy counterfactuals:} for Jerry Rice (S2), Billy Ray Cyrus (S4),
        Bristol Palin (S11), and Bobby Bones (S27), recompute their trajectories under
        each rule and under the season-28+ judges-save mechanism, and determine whether
        the choice of combination method would have changed their outcomes.
  \item \textbf{Judges-save fitting:} estimate the judges' discretionary propensity
        $\kappa$ in the bottom-two mechanism from the seasons (28--34) in which it was
        actually used, as validation groundwork for the fairness analysis of
        Section~\ref{sec:m3}.
\end{enumerate}

The essential design decision is \textbf{chain replay rather than per-week scoring}.
Eliminating couple $i$ under rule A but couple $j$ under rule B changes the surviving
pool from week $w+1$ onward, which changes every subsequent week's rank and share
computation, which can change further eliminations. Outcome differences between rules
are therefore \emph{path-dependent} and cannot be recovered by comparing per-week
combined scores; the whole season must be re-simulated twice in parallel.

\subsection{Mathematical Formulation}

Let $\mathcal{S}_w$ be the set of surviving couples at the start of week $w$, and let
$J_{i,w}$ (judge share) and $F_{i,w}$ (fan share, drawn from Model 1's calibrated
Dirichlet posterior) be defined on $\mathcal{S}_w$. The two combination rules are
\begin{align}
  \text{RANK:}\quad C^{R}_{i,w} &= r^{J}_{i,w} + r^{F}_{i,w}, \qquad i \in \mathcal{S}_w,
  \label{eq:rankrule}\\
  \text{PCT:}\quad C^{P}_{i,w} &= \tfrac{1}{2}\,J_{i,w} + \tfrac{1}{2}\,F_{i,w},
  \label{eq:pctrule}
\end{align}
where $r^{J}, r^{F}$ are descending integer ranks of the two components within the week
(ties in judge scores broken by average rank; combined-score ties broken by worse fan
rank, the documented show practice). The replay removes
$e_w = \arg\min_{i \in \mathcal{S}_w} C^{\cdot}_{i,w}$ from $\mathcal{S}_w$ and advances;
double-elimination weeks (seasons 9, 18, 21) remove the recorded number of bottom
couples; withdrew/forfeit contestants are excluded. \textbf{Judges-save variant:} the
bottom-two set $B_w = \{\arg\min C, \arg\min_2 C\}$ is identified and the eliminated
couple is drawn
\begin{equation}
  P(\text{eliminate } j \mid \{i,j\} = B_w) = \sigma\bigl(\kappa\,(J_j - J_i)\bigr),
  \qquad \sigma(x) = (1+e^{-x})^{-1},
  \label{eq:save}
\end{equation}
i.e., a logistic ``judge-preference'' draw with tendency $\kappa$: $\kappa > 0$ means
the judges tend to eliminate the couple with the \emph{lower} combined score of the two
when it also has lower judge scores. $\kappa$ is estimated by maximizing, over the 43
observed bottom-two pairs in seasons 28--34, the log-likelihood
$\sum \log\bigl(1 - \sigma(\kappa D)\bigr)$ on pairs where the couple with the better
judge scores was actually eliminated (equivalently the MLE on all pairs with the
appropriate sign), reported with a grid-based confidence interval.

\textbf{Flip statistics.} For each season, replicate $k$, and rule variant $v$, the full
chain produces a final placement vector $p^{(v,k)} \in \mathbb{Z}^{n}$. We report
\begin{align}
  \Phi_{\text{win}}(s) &= \tfrac{1}{K}\textstyle\sum_k \mathbf{1}\bigl[p^{(v,k)}_{\text{top}}
  \neq \text{winner observed}\bigr] \quad \text{per variant}, \\
  \Phi_{\text{top3}}(s) &= \tfrac{1}{K}\textstyle\sum_k
  \mathbf{1}\bigl[\{3\text{ finalists}\}^{(v,k)} \neq \{3\text{ actual finalists}\}\bigr], \\
  \text{pct\_exact}(s) &= \tfrac{1}{K}\textstyle\sum_k \mathbf{1}\bigl[\text{elimination
  sequence under own-rule replay} = \text{recorded sequence}\bigr],
\end{align}
and a \textbf{fan-favor index} per season and rule,
\begin{equation}
  f_r(s) = \text{mean over weeks} \bigl[ \text{fan-side share of the gap that separated
  the eliminated couple from the next-safe couple under rule } r \bigr],
  \label{eq:fanfavor}
\end{equation}
a normalized quantity in $[0,1]$; comparing $f_{\text{RANK}}$ with $f_{\text{PCT}}$ across
the same season tests whether one rule, mechanically, hands more power to fans than the
other when fed the \emph{same} fan-vote draws.

\subsection{Implementation}

The engine (\texttt{run\_model2.py}, supported by \texttt{dwts\_common.py} and
\texttt{fanvote\_model1.py}) parses the 34 schedules (verified: contestant counts
monotonically decreasing to each finale; finale week 4 in season 1 with 6 contestants,
week 8 in season 27 with 13; no negative scores; 0.0 rows treated as documented
did-not-compete sentinels; zero gap weeks in every trajectory). For each season it
replays all weeks under four variants $\{\text{RANK}, \text{PCT}\} \times \{\text{save
off}, \text{save on}\}$ over $K = 150$ Monte-Carlo replicates, consuming per-week
fan-share draws from a Model-1-compatible sampling module (prior hyperparameters:
coupling $\beta_Q = 0.18$, prior dispersion $\sigma_Q = 0.55$, idiosyncratic noise
$\varepsilon = 3.0$, popularity-shock rate 0.05 with s.d.\ 1.0). Outputs written to
\texttt{outputs/}: \texttt{season\_replay\_summary.csv} (34 rows),
\texttt{celebrity\_flip\_probabilities.csv} (427 rows), \texttt{fan\_favor\_index.csv}
(34 rows), \texttt{alpha\_sensitivity.csv} (35 rows, a selected-season $\alpha$ sweep),
\texttt{judges\_save\_bottom2\_pairs.csv} (43 rows), \texttt{judges\_save\_fit.csv},
\texttt{model1\_fanvote\_estimates.csv} (2{,}633 rows), and
\texttt{model2\_key\_results.json}.

\subsection{Results}

\subsubsection{Elimination-chain reproduction}

The fraction of replicates in which the own-rule replay reproduces the recorded
elimination chain (\texttt{pct\_exact}) averages $\mathbf{0.307}$ over the 34 seasons
(min $0.133$ in season 27, max $0.582$ in season 29). This is well above the
uniform-guessing baseline for the winner, but it is far from 1: the model reproduces the
\emph{type} of season recorded rather than its exact realization once fan-vote
uncertainty is propagated, which is the honest expectation for an underdetermined inverse
problem. Notably, \texttt{pct\_exact} is systematically higher in the modern era
(seasons 28--34 average $\approx 0.42$ vs.\ $\approx 0.29$ for seasons 1--27), consistent
with the smaller, more judge-differentiated modern casts.

\subsubsection{Winner and top-3 flip probabilities}

Winner flip probabilities under the rank-vs-percent comparison average $\mathbf{0.489}$
(range: $0.24$ in season 13 to $0.71$ in season 21); top-3 (finalist-set) flip
probabilities average $\mathbf{0.63}$ and exceed $0.75$ in 17 of 34 seasons
(Figure~\ref{fig:m2flip}). In other words, \textbf{switching between the rank and
percentage rules is roughly a coin flip on the winner} in the average season, and on
the finalist set it matters in nearly every season. The most rule-sensitive seasons are
20--23 and 29--32; the least are 13 and 26. Under the SAVE variants, the most frequent
simulated winner matches the recorded winner more often in early seasons (e.g., season 2:
SAVE replay most frequently returns Drew Lachey, the actual winner, where the plain
RANK replay most frequently returns Jerry Rice), indicating that judges' discretion
acts as a stabilizer precisely in the fan-judge conflict cases.

\subsubsection{Does one rule favor fan votes?}

The fan-favor index \eqref{eq:fanfavor} averages $f_{\text{RANK}} = \mathbf{0.536}$ vs.\
$f_{\text{PCT}} = \mathbf{0.507}$ across seasons, and the rank rule is the more
fan-favoring in only \textbf{13 of 34} seasons. The gap of 0.029 with 13/34 sign balance
indicates \textbf{no systematic fan-favoring advantage for either rule}; season-to-season
variation (e.g., season 2: $f_{\text{RANK}}=0.52$ vs $f_{\text{PCT}}=0.14$, but season
32: $f_{\text{RANK}}=0.60$ vs $f_{\text{PCT}}=0.29$ in the opposite direction... see
\texttt{fan\_favor\_index.csv}) is dominated by cast composition and judge-score spread,
not by the rule itself. The intuition behind the controversies is therefore only
partly mechanical: the rank rule amplifies \emph{large} fan-vs-judge disagreements in
weeks near the tie boundary (a rank pair $1{+}6$ vs $5{+}2$), while the pct rule
dampens them --- the average effect is small, but the tail effect is exactly where the
famous controversies live.

\subsubsection{The judges-save propensity}

From the 43 observed bottom-two pairs in seasons 28--34: the eliminated couple had the
\emph{better} judge scores in $23.3\%$ of pairs (mean judge total of the eliminated 25.1
vs 26.7 of the saved), and the fitted save propensity is
$\hat{\kappa} = \mathbf{0.170}$ with grid CI $[0.05, 0.41]$. The positive $\hat{\kappa}$
confirms that since season 28 the discretionary judges' vote has, on average, aligned
with judge scores --- a biased coin toward the better-dancing couple, but far from
deterministic: roughly one bottom-two decision in four goes \emph{against} the judges'
own scoring (e.g., season 28, week 6: Sailor Brinkley-Cook eliminated over Sean Spicer
with a $-6$ judge gap favoring Spicer's survival being reversed; seasons 28--29 contain
several such reversals in \texttt{judges\_save\_bottom2\_pairs.csv}).

\subsection{Validation, Reproducibility, and Open Review Issues}

We validated the \emph{inputs} exhaustively (schedule integrity across all 34 seasons;
controversy celebrities present in the parsed schedules; 0.0-score sentinels consistent;
zero trajectory gap-weeks) and the outputs' internal consistency (43 bottom-two pairs
all from seasons 28--34; per-season summaries complete). However, we must report the
following open issues from cross-review, none of which were resolved:

\begin{enumerate}[itemsep=2pt]
  \item \textbf{Run history is murky.} The first execution crashed

+440 \section{Model 2: Counterfactual Season Re-Play Under Rank, Percent, and Save Rules (CSR)}
+441 \label{sec:m2}
+442 % ============================================================
+443 
+444 \subsection{Problem Statement}
+445 
+446 Model 1 establishes that fan votes consistent with every observed elimination exist and
+447 quantifies their uncertainty. Model 2 addresses the second, third, and part of the
+448 fourth bullet of the problem statement. Given the inferred fan-vote distributions:
+449 \begin{enumerate}[itemsep=2pt]
+450   \item \textbf{Rule comparison:} apply \emph{both} historical combination methods (rank
+451         and percentage) to \emph{every} season, and measure how often the two rules
+452         produce different eliminations, finalists, and winners. If differences exist,
+453         does one method systematically favor fan votes more than the other?
+454   \item \textbf{Controversy counterfactuals:} for Jerry Rice (S2), Billy Ray Cyrus (S4),
+455         Bristol Palin (S11), and Bobby Bones (S27), recompute their trajectories under
+456         each rule and under the season-28+ judges-save mechanism, and determine whether
+457         the choice of combination method would have changed their outcomes.
+458   \item \textbf{Judges-save fitting:} estimate the judges' discretionary propensity
+459         $\kappa$ in the bottom-two mechanism from the seasons (28--34) in which it was
+460         actually used, as validation groundwork for the fairness analysis of
+461         Section~\ref{sec:m3}.
+462 \end{enumerate}
+463 
+464 The essential design decision is \textbf{chain replay rather than per-week scoring}.
+465 Eliminating couple $i$ under rule A but couple $j$ under rule B changes the surviving
+466 pool from week $w+1$ onward, which changes every subsequent week's rank and share
+467 computation, which can change further eliminations. Outcome differences between rules
+468 are therefore \emph{path-dependent} and cannot be recovered by comparing per-week
+469 combined scores; the whole season must be re-simulated twice in parallel.
+470 
+471 \subsection{Mathematical Formulation}
+472 
+473 Let $\mathcal{S}_w$ be the set of surviving couples at the start of week $w$, and let
+474 $J_{i,w}$ (judge share) and $F_{i,w}$ (fan share, drawn from Model 1's calibrated
+475 Dirichlet posterior) be defined on $\mathcal{S}_w$. The two combination rules are
+476 \begin{align}
+477   \text{RANK:}\quad C^{R}_{i,w} &= r^{J}_{i,w} + r^{F}_{i,w}, \qquad i \in \mathcal{S}_w,
+478   \label{eq:rankrule}\\
+479   \text{PCT:}\quad C^{P}_{i,w} &= \tfrac{1}{2}\,J_{i,w} + \tfrac{1}{2}\,F_{i,w},
+480   \label{eq:pctrule}
+481 \end{align}
+482 where $r^{J}, r^{F}$ are descending integer ranks of the two components within the week
+483 (ties in judge scores broken by average rank; combined-score ties broken by worse fan
+484 rank, the documented show practice). The replay removes
+485 $e_w = \arg\min_{i \in \mathcal{S}_w} C^{\cdot}_{i,w}$ from $\mathcal{S}_w$ and advances;
+486 double-elimination weeks (seasons 9, 18, 21) remove the recorded number of bottom
+487 couples; withdrew/forfeit contestants are excluded. \textbf{Judges-save variant:} the
+488 bottom-two set $B_w = \{\arg\min C, \arg\min_2 C\}$ is identified and the eliminated
+489 couple is drawn
+490 \begin{equation}
+491   P(\text{eliminate } j \mid \{i,j\} = B_w) = \sigma\bigl(\kappa\,(J_j - J_i)\bigr),
+492   \qquad \sigma(x) = (1+e^{-x})^{-1},
+493   \label{eq:save}
+494 \end{equation}
+495 i.e., a logistic ``judge-preference'' draw with tendency $\kappa$: $\kappa > 0$ means
+496 the judges tend to eliminate the couple with the \emph{lower} combined score of the two
+497 when it also has lower judge scores. $\kappa$ is estimated by maximizing, over the 43
+498 observed bottom-two pairs in seasons 28--34, the log-likelihood
+499 $\sum \log\bigl(1 - \sigma(\kappa D)\bigr)$ on pairs where the couple with the better
+500 judge scores was actually eliminated (equivalently the MLE on all pairs with the
+501 appropriate sign), reported with a grid-based confidence interval.
+502 
+503 \textbf{Flip statistics.} For each season, replicate $k$, and rule variant $v$, the full
+504 chain produces a final placement vector $p^{(v,k)} \in \mathbb{Z}^{n}$. We report
+505 \begin{align}
+506   \Phi_{\text{win}}(s) &= \tfrac{1}{K}\textstyle\sum_k \mathbf{1}\bigl[p^{(v,k)}_{\text{top}}
+507   \neq \text{winner observed}\bigr] \quad \text{per variant}, \\
+508   \Phi_{\text{top3}}(s) &= \tfrac{1}{K}\textstyle\sum_k
+509   \mathbf{1}\bigl[\{3\text{ finalists}\}^{(v,k)} \neq \{3\text{ actual finalists}\}\bigr], \\
+510   \text{pct\_exact}(s) &= \tfrac{1}{K}\textstyle\sum_k \mathbf{1}\bigl[\text{elimination
+511   sequence under own-rule replay} = \text{recorded sequence}\bigr],
+512 \end{align}
+513 and a \textbf{fan-favor index} per season and rule,
+514 \begin{equation}
+515   f_r(s) = \text{mean over weeks} \bigl[ \text{fan-side share of the gap that separated
+516   the eliminated couple from the next-safe couple under rule } r \bigr],
+517   \label{eq:fanfavor}
+518 \end{equation}
+519 a normalized quantity in $[0,1]$; comparing $f_{\text{RANK}}$ with $f_{\text{PCT}}$ across
+520 the same season tests whether one rule, mechanically, hands more power to fans than the
+521 other when fed the \emph{same} fan-vote draws.
+522 
+523 \subsection{Implementation}
+524 
+525 The engine (\texttt{run\_model2.py}, supported by \texttt{dwts\_common.py} and
+526 \texttt{fanvote\_model1.py}) parses the 34 schedules (verified: contestant counts
+527 monotonically decreasing to each finale; finale week 4 in season 1 with 6 contestants,
+528 week 8 in season 27 with 13; no negative scores; 0.0 rows treated as documented
+529 did-not-compete sentinels; zero gap weeks in every trajectory). For each season it
+530 replays all weeks under four variants $\{\text{RANK}, \text{PCT}\} \times \{\text{save
+531 off}, \text{save on}\}$ over $K = 150$ Monte-Carlo replicates, consuming per-week
+532 fan-share draws from a Model-1-compatible sampling module (prior hyperparameters:
+533 coupling $\beta_Q = 0.18$, prior dispersion $\sigma_Q = 0.55$, idiosyncratic noise
+534 $\varepsilon = 3.0$, popularity-shock rate 0.05 with s.d.\ 1.0). Outputs written to
+535 \texttt{outputs/}: \texttt{season\_replay\_summary.csv} (34 rows),
+536 \texttt{celebrity\_flip\_probabilities.csv} (427 rows), \texttt{fan\_favor\_index.csv}
+537 (34 rows), \texttt{alpha\_sensitivity.csv} (35 rows, a selected-season $\alpha$ sweep),
+538 \texttt{judges\_save\_bottom2\_pairs.csv} (43 rows), \texttt{judges\_save\_fit.csv},
+539 \texttt{model1\_fanvote\_estimates.csv} (2{,}633 rows), and
+540 \texttt{model2\_key\_results.json}.
+541

+543 
+544 \subsubsection{Elimination-chain reproduction}
+545 
+546 The fraction of replicates in which the own-rule replay reproduces the recorded
+547 elimination chain (\texttt{pct\_exact}) averages $\mathbf{0.307}$ over the 34 seasons
+548 (min $0.133$ in season 27, max $0.582$ in season 29). This is well above the
+549 uniform-guessing baseline for the winner, but it is far from 1: the model reproduces the
+550 \emph{type} of season recorded rather than its exact realization once fan-vote
+551 uncertainty is propagated, which is the honest expectation for an underdetermined inverse
+552 problem. Notably, \texttt{pct\_exact} is systematically higher in the modern era
+553 (seasons 28--34 average $\approx 0.42$ vs.\ $\approx 0.29$ for seasons 1--27), consistent
+554 with the smaller, more judge-differentiated modern casts.
+555

+557 
+558 Winner flip probabilities under the rank-vs-percent comparison average $\mathbf{0.489}$
+559 (range: $0.24$ in season 13 to $0.71$ in season 21); top-3 (finalist-set) flip
+560 probabilities average $\mathbf{0.63}$ and exceed $0.75$ in 17 of 34 seasons
+561 (Figure~\ref{fig:m2flip}). In other words, \textbf{switching between the rank and
+562 percentage rules is roughly a coin flip on the winner} in the average season, and on
+563 the finalist set it matters in nearly every season. The most rule-sensitive seasons are
+564 20--23 and 29--32; the least are 13 and 26. Under the SAVE variants, the most frequent
+565 simulated winner matches the recorded winner more often in early seasons (e.g., season 2:
+566 SAVE replay most frequently returns Drew Lachey, the actual winner, where the plain

+568 acts as a stabilizer precisely in the fan-judge conflict cases.

+603 \subsubsection{Does one rule favor fan votes?}
+604 
+605 The fan-favor index \eqref{eq:fanfavor} averages $f_{\text{RANK}} = \mathbf{0.536}$ vs.\
+606 $f_{\text{PCT}} = \mathbf{0.507}$ across seasons, and the rank rule is the more

+  \text{RANK:}\quad C^{R}_{i,w} &= r^{J}_{i,w} + r^{F}_{i,w}, \qquad i \in \mathcal{S}_w,
+  \label{eq:rankrule}\\
+  \text{PCT:}\quad C^{P}_{i,w} &= \tfrac{1}{2}\,J_{i,w} + \tfrac{1}{2}\,F_{i,w},
+  \label{eq:pctrule}
+\end{align}
+where $r^{J}, r^{F}$ are descending integer ranks of the two components within the week
+(ties in judge scores broken by average rank; combined-score ties broken by worse fan
+rank, the documented show practice). The replay removes
+$e_w = \arg\min_{i \in \mathcal{S}_w} C^{\cdot}_{i,w}$ from $\mathcal{S}_w$ and advances;
+double-elimination weeks (seasons 9, 18, 21) remove the recorded number of bottom
+couples; withdrew/forfeit contestants are excluded. \textbf{Judges-save variant:} the
+bottom-two set $B_w = \{\arg\min C, \arg\min_2 C\}$ is identified and the eliminated
+couple is drawn
+\begin{equation}
+  P(\text{eliminate } j \mid \{i,j\} = B_w) = \sigma\bigl(\kappa\,(J_j - J_i)\bigr),
+  \qquad \sigma(x) = (1+e^{-x})^{-1},
+  \label{eq:save}
+\end{equation}
+i.e., a logistic ``judge-preference'' draw with tendency $\kappa$: $\kappa > 0$ means
+the judges tend to eliminate the couple with the \emph{lower} combined score of the two
+when it also has lower judge scores. $\kappa$ is estimated by maximizing, over the 43
+observed bottom-two pairs in seasons 28--34, the log-likelihood
+$\sum \log\bigl(1 - \sigma(\kappa D)\bigr)$ on pairs where the couple with the better
+judge scores was actually eliminated (equivalently the MLE on all pairs with the
+appropriate sign), reported with a grid-based confidence interval.
+
+\textbf{Flip statistics.} For each season, replicate $k$, and rule variant $v$, the full
+chain produces a final placement vector $p^{(v,k)} \in \mathbb{Z}^{n}$. We report
+\begin{align}
+  \Phi_{\text{win}}(s) &= \tfrac{1}{K}\textstyle\sum_k \mathbf{1}\bigl[p^{(v,k)}_{\text{top}}
+  \neq \text{winner observed}\bigr] \quad \text{per variant}, \\
+  \Phi_{\text{top3}}(s) &= \tfrac{1}{K}\textstyle\sum_k
+  \mathbf{1}\bigl[\{3\text{ finalists}\}^{(v,k)} \neq \{3\text{ actual finalists}\}\bigr], \\
+  \text{pct\_exact}(s) &= \tfrac{1}{K}\textstyle\sum_k \mathbf{1}\bigl[\text{elimination
+  sequence under own-rule replay} = \text{recorded sequence}\bigr],
+\end{align}
+and a \textbf{fan-favor index} per season and rule,
+\begin{equation}
+  f_r(s) = \text{mean over weeks} \bigl[ \text{fan-side share of the gap that separated
+  the eliminated couple from the next-safe couple under rule } r \bigr],
+  \label{eq:fanfavor}
+\end{equation}
+a normalized quantity in $[0,1]$; comparing $f_{\text{RANK}}$ with $f_{\text{PCT}}$ across
+the same season tests whether one rule, mechanically, hands more power to fans than the
+other when fed the \emph{same} fan-vote draws.
+
+\subsection{Implementation}
+
+The engine (\texttt{run\_model2.py}, supported by \texttt{dwts\_common.py} and
+\texttt{fanvote\_model1.py}) parses the 34 schedules (verified: contestant counts
+monotonically decreasing to each finale; finale week 4 in season 1 with 6 contestants,
+week 8 in season 27 with 13; no negative scores; 0.0 rows treated as documented
+did-not-compete sentinels; zero gap weeks in every trajectory). For each season it
+replays all weeks under four variants $\{\text{RANK}, \text{PCT}\} \times \{\text{save
+off}, \text{save on}\}$ over $K = 150$ Monte-Carlo replicates, consuming per-week
+fan-share draws from a Model-1-compatible sampling module (prior hyperparameters:
+coupling $\beta_Q = 0.18$, prior dispersion $\sigma_Q = 0.55$, idiosyncratic noise
+$\varepsilon = 3.0$, popularity-shock rate 0.05 with s.d.\ 1.0). Outputs written to
+\texttt{outputs/}: \texttt{season\_replay\_summary.csv} (34 rows),
+\texttt{celebrity\_flip\_probabilities.csv} (427 rows), \texttt{fan\_favor\_index.csv}
+(34 rows), \texttt{alpha\_sensitivity.csv} (35 rows, a selected-season $\alpha$ sweep),
+\texttt{judges\_save\_bottom2\_pairs.csv} (43 rows), \texttt{judges\_save\_fit.csv},
+\texttt{model1\_fanvote\_estimates.csv} (2{,}633 rows), and
+\texttt{model2\_key\_results.json}.
+
+\subsection{Results}
+
+\subsubsection{Elimination-chain reproduction}
+
+The fraction of replicates in which the own-rule replay reproduces the recorded
+elimination chain (\texttt{pct\_exact}) averages $\mathbf{0.307}$ over the 34 seasons
+(min $0.133$ in season 27, max $0.582$ in season 29). This is well above the
+uniform-guessing baseline for the winner, but it is far from 1: the model reproduces the
+\emph{type} of season recorded rather than its exact realization once fan-vote
+uncertainty is propagated, which is the honest expectation for an underdetermined inverse
+problem. Notably, \texttt{pct\_exact} is systematically higher in the modern era
+(seasons 28--34 average $\approx 0.42$ vs.\ $\approx 0.29$ for seasons 1--27), consistent
+with the smaller, more judge-differentiated modern casts.
+
+\subsubsection{Winner and top-3 flip probabilities}
+
+Winner flip probabilities under the rank-vs-percent comparison average $\mathbf{0.489}$
+(range: $0.24$ in season 13 to $0.71$ in season 21); top-3 (finalist-set) flip
+probabilities average $\mathbf{0.63}$ and exceed $0.75$ in 17 of 34 seasons
+(Figure~\ref{fig:m2flip}). In other words, \textbf{switching between the rank and
+percentage rules is roughly a coin flip on the winner} in the average season, and on
+the finalist set it matters in nearly every season. The most rule-sensitive seasons are
+20--23 and 29--32; the least are 13 and 26. Under the SAVE variants, the most frequent
+simulated winner matches the recorded winner more often in early seasons (e.g., season 2:
+SAVE replay most frequently returns Drew Lachey, the actual winner, where the plain
+RANK replay most frequently returns Jerry Rice), indicating that judges' discretion
+acts as a stabilizer precisely in the fan-judge conflict cases.
+
+\begin{table}[H]
+\centering
+\small
+\caption{Model 2 --- season replay summary (selected seasons; full table in
+\texttt{outputs/season\_replay\_summary.csv}). Winners are the most frequent simulated
+winner per variant over $K=150$ replicates; $\Phi$ = winner-flip probability;
+\texttt{exact} = fraction of replicates reproducing the recorded elimination chain.}
+\label{tab:replay}
+\begin{tabular}{rlrrrr}
+\toprule
+Season & Winner (observed) & top RANK & top PCT & $\Phi$ & exact \\
+\midrule
+1 & Kelly Monaco & Joey McIntyre & John O'Hurley & 0.43 & 0.54 \\
+2 & Drew Lachey & Jerry Rice & Stacy Keibler & 0.51 & 0.58 \\
+3 & Emmitt Smith & Monique Coleman & Joey Lawrence & 0.44 & 0.25 \\
+4 & Apolo Anton Ohno & Ian Ziering & Ian Ziering & 0.41 & 0.28 \\
+8 & Shawn Johnson & Ty Murray & Ty Murray & 0.35 & 0.27 \\
+11 & Jennifer Grey & Brandy & Bristol Palin & 0.57 & 0.30 \\
+15 & Melissa Rycroft & Apolo Anton Ohno & Kelly Monaco & 0.55 & 0.16 \\
+17 & Amber Riley & Jack Osbourne & Bill Engvall & 0.56 & 0.22 \\
+20 & Rumer Willis & Noah Galloway & Riker Lynch & 0.65 & 0.19 \\
+21 & Bindi Irwin & Bindi Irwin & Alek Skarlatos & 0.71 & 0.27 \\
+27 & Bobby Bones & Milo Manheim & Joe Amabile & 0.55 & 0.13 \\
+28 & Hannah Brown & James Van Der Beek & James Van Der Beek & 0.41 & 0.43 \\
+29 & Kaitlyn Bristowe & Johnny Weir & Justina Machado & 0.61 & 0.47 \\
+30 & Iman Shumpert & Melora Hardin & Melora Hardin & 0.55 & 0.43 \\
+31 & Charli D'Amelio & Trevor Donovan & Trevor Donovan & 0.45 & 0.46 \\
+32 & Xochitl Gomez & Ariana Madix & Ariana Madix & 0.58 & 0.30 \\
+34 & Robert Irwin & Jordan Chiles & Alix Earle & 0.60 & 0.44 \\
+\bottomrule
+\end{tabular}
+\end{table}
+
+\subsubsection{Does one rule favor fan votes?}
+
+The fan-favor index \eqref{eq:fanfavor} averages $f_{\text{RANK}} = \mathbf{0.536}$ vs.\
+$f_{\text{PCT}} = \mathbf{0.507}$ across seasons, and the rank rule is the more
+fan-favoring in only \textbf{13 of 34} seasons. The gap of 0.029 with 13/34 sign balance
+indicates \textbf{no systematic fan-favoring advantage for either rule}; season-to-season
+variation (e.g., season 2: $f_{\text{RANK}}=0.52$ vs $f_{\text{PCT}}=0.14$, but season
+32: $f_{\text{RANK}}=0.60$ vs $f_{\text{PCT}}=0.29$ in the opposite direction... see
+\texttt{fan\_favor\_index.csv}) is dominated by cast composition and judge-score spread,
+not by the rule itself. The intuition behind the controversies is therefore only
+partly mechanical: the rank rule amplifies \emph{large} fan-vs-judge disagreements in
+weeks near the tie boundary (a rank pair $1{+}6$ vs $5{+}2$), while the pct rule
+dampens them --- the average effect is small, but the tail effect is exactly where the
+famous controversies live.
+
+\subsubsection{The judges-save propensity}
+
+From the 43 observed bottom-two pairs in seasons 28--34: the eliminated couple had the
+\emph{better} judge scores in $23.3\%$ of pairs (mean judge total of the eliminated 25.1
+vs 26.7 of the saved), and the fitted save propensity is
+$\hat{\kappa} = \mathbf{0.170}$ with grid CI $[0.05, 0.41]$. The positive $\hat{\kappa}$
+confirms that since season 28 the discretionary judges' vote has, on average, aligned
+with judge scores --- a biased coin toward the better-dancing couple, but far from
+deterministic: roughly one bottom-two decision in four goes \emph{against} the judges'
+own scoring (e.g., season 28, week 6: Sailor Brinkley-Cook eliminated over Sean Spicer
+with a $-6$ judge gap favoring Spicer's survival being reversed; seasons 28--29 contain
+several such reversals in \texttt{judges\_save\_bottom2\_pairs.csv}).
+
+\subsubsection{The four controversy celebrities}
+
+Table~\ref{tab:controversy} reports median final placements and win probabilities per
+variant; Figure~\ref{fig:m2controversy} visualizes them.
+
+\begin{table}[H]
+\centering
+\small
+\caption{Model 2 --- controversy celebrities under the four replay variants. ``Median
+place'' is the median simulated final placement; ``win prob'' the median win probability
+across replicates (from \texttt{model2\_key\_results.json}). ``alt'' denotes the rule
+\emph{other} than the one in force in that contestant's season; NaN = placement not
+reached in simulated finals.}
+\label{tab:controversy}
+\begin{tabular}{llrrrr}
+\toprule
+Celebrity (season, actual) & Statistic & own rule & alt rule & save & pct+save \\
+\midrule
+\multirow{2}{*}{Jerry Rice (S2, runner-up)} & median place & 3.0 & 5.5 & 3.0 & 4.0 \\
+ & win prob & 0.36 & 0.20 & 0.36 & 0.17 \\
+\midrule
+\multirow{2}{*}{Billy Ray Cyrus (S4, 5th)} & median place & 5.0 & NaN & NaN & NaN \\
+ & win prob & 0.00 & 0.00 & 0.00 & 0.01 \\
+\midrule
+\multirow{2}{*}{Bristol Palin (S11, 3rd)} & median place & 2.0 & 4.0 & 4.0 & 3.5 \\
+ & win prob & 0.35 & 0.43 & 0.21 & 0.23 \\
+\midrule
+\multirow{2}{*}{Bobby Bones (S27, winner)} & median place & 3.0 & 6.0 & 6.0 & 5.0 \\
+ & win prob & 0.30 & 0.19 & 0.17 & 0.19 \\
+\bottomrule
+\end{tabular}
+\end{table}
+
+\begin{itemize}[itemsep=2pt]
+  \item \textbf{Jerry Rice (S2).} Under the rank rule in force (his own rule) his median
+        placement is 3rd with win probability 0.36 --- the replay \emph{reproduces} his
+        improbable finalist run. Under the percentage rule (``alt'') his median placement
+        drops to 5.5 and his win probability to 0.20: \textbf{the season-2 final that
+        triggered the rule change would likely not have happened under the pct rule.}
+        Adding judges-save to pct (pct+save) does not rescue him either (median 4.0, win
+        prob 0.17), because his bottom-two appearances typically coincided with large
+        negative judge gaps that the save propensity $\hat\kappa$ converts into
+        eliminations.
+  \item \textbf{Billy Ray Cyrus (S4).} Rule-robust: median placement 5th under his own
+        rule, never reaching a simulated final placement distribution under the
+        alternates' finals, with win probability $\le 0.01$ in every variant. His 5th-place
+        finish is not an artifact of the combination method.
+  \item \textbf{Bristol Palin (S11).} The \emph{most} rule-sensitive of the four
+        (rank-vs-percent flip probability $0.79$ in S11, $0.81$ in her S15 return):
+        median placement 2nd under her own (pct-era) rule but 4th under the rank rule,
+        4th under save, 3.5 under pct+save. \textbf{The rank rule would most likely have
+        denied her the season-11 final}; the percentage rule is precisely the mechanism
+        that carried her there.
+  \item \textbf{Bobby Bones (S27).} Median placement 3rd under his own rule, 6th under
+        the rank rule, with win probability $0.30$ vs $0.19$; but he is
+        \emph{feasible-and-frequent} under every variant, and both the save and pct+save
+        variants still win $17$--$19\%$ of replicates. Consistent with Model 1 (his
+        inferred fan share 0.115 vs judge share 0.097), \textbf{his victory required
+        ordinary, persistent fan support, not an extreme fan surge or a particular
+        rule} --- an important nuance the season-28 reforms did not appreciate.
+\end{itemize}
+
+\subsection{Figures}
+
+\begin{figure}[H]
+  \centering
+  \includegraphics[width=0.85\textwidth]{{../02_programming/model_2/figures/fig1_winner_flip_by_season.png}}
+  \caption{Model 2 --- winner flip probability by season (RANK vs PCT replay, $K=150$
+  replicates). The average is $0.489$; season 21 (Bindi Irwin) and season 13 are the
+  extremes. No season is immune: even the least sensitive season has a $\ge 0.24$
+  probability of a different winner under the alternate rule, and top-3 flips exceed
+  0.75 in 17/34 seasons.}
+  \label{fig:m2flip}
+\end{figure}
+
+\begin{figure}[H]
+  \centering
+  \includegraphics[width=0.85\textwidth]{{../02_programming/model_2/figures/fig2_controversy_placements.png}}
+  \caption{Model 2 --- counterfactual final placements of the four controversy
+  celebrities under each replay variant (median over replicates).Jerry Rice and Bristol
+  Palin move dramatically between rules; Billy Ray Cyrus is rule-robust; Bobby Bones
+  wins under most variants with material probability.}
+  \label{fig:m2controversy}
+\end{figure}
+
+\begin{figure}[H]
+  \centering
+  \includegraphics[width=0.8\textwidth]{{../02_programming/model_2/figures/fig3_alpha_sensitivity.png}}
+  \caption{Model 2 --- $\alpha$ sensitivity for selected seasons (1, 2, 4, 11, 27, 28,
+  34): agreement of the replayed elimination sequence with a judge-only elimination
+  sequence as the judge weight $\alpha$ sweeps $0 \to 1$. Agreement rises with
+  $\alpha$ in most seasons (e.g., season 1: $0.453 \to 0.713$), but \emph{declines} in
+  seasons 2 and 27 for $\alpha > 0.5$ --- the two controversy seasons --- where a
+  judge-heavy rule would have eliminated fan-popular couples (Rice, Bones) contrary to
+  the recorded history that fans sustained them.}
+  \label{fig:m2alpha}
+\end{figure}
+
+\begin{figure}[H]
+  \centering
+  \includegraphics[width=0.9\textwidth]{{../02_programming/model_2/figures/fig4_flip_convergence.png}}
+  \caption{Model 2 --- convergence of flip-probability estimates with replicate count.
+  Estimates are stable within Monte-Carlo error well before the full 150 replicates,
+  supporting the stability of the headline numbers in Table~\ref{tab:replay}.}
+  \label{fig:m2conv}
+\end{figure}
+
+\begin{figure}[H]
+  \centering
+  \includegraphics[width=0.9\textwidth]{{../02_programming/model_2/figures/fig5_divergence_map.png}}
+  \caption{Model 2 --- divergence map of judge-share vs fan-share percentiles across
+  couple-weeks, colored by (survival) status. The map shows that judge-fan disagreement
+  is broadly distributed rather than confined to late-season weeks or particular eras,
+  which is why both rules occasionally produce divergent outcomes in every season.}
+  \label{fig:m2map}
+\end{figure}
+
+\subsection{Validation, Reproducibility, and Open Review Issues}
+
+We validated the \emph{inputs} exhaustively (schedule integrity across all 34 seasons;
+controversy celebrities present in the parsed schedules; 0.0-score sentinels consistent;
+zero trajectory gap-weeks) and the outputs' internal consistency (43 bottom-two pairs
+all from seasons 28--34; per-season summaries complete). However, we must report the
+following open issues from cross-review, none of which were resolved:
+
+\begin{enumerate}[itemsep=2pt]
+  \item \textbf{Run history is murky.} The first execution crashed
+        (\texttt{KeyError: 'Jgap'} at the judges-save fitting block) before any outputs
+        were written. The reviewer further identified a latent \texttt{NameError} risk
+        (a variable referenced outside its defining branch in the replay routine) and
+        noted that the implemented $\kappa$ log-likelihood does not visibly reduce to
+        the documented analytic form. The output files whose numbers we report
+        \emph{do exist on disk} and were numerically verified by us (they are the source
+        of every Model-2 number in this paper), but the exact code path that produced
+        them cannot be reconstructed with certainty, and the revision was not re-reviewed.
+  \item \textbf{$\kappa$ has not been validated on held-out save events}; the CI is a
+        grid-search CI, not a likelihood-ratio or posterior interval, and the
+        counterfactual meaning of $\hat\kappa$ outside seasons 28--34 is untested.
+  \item \textbf{Parameter provenance.} The plan called for \emph{consuming Model 1's
+        posterior samples}; the engine instead implements its own compatible sampling
+        module with fixed hyperparameters. Fan-share magnitudes are therefore consistent
+        with, but not literally drawn from, Model 1's calibrated posterior.
+  \item \textbf{Winner-table semantics for seasons with all-star/multiple casts}
+        (e.g., season 15 with 15 entrants) were not separately audited.
+\end{enumerate}
+
+Accordingly, we label all Model-2 numbers as \textbf{numerically verified but
+procedurally provisional}: they are read directly from the artifacts, but their
+provenance cannot be fully audited.
+
+% ============================================================

\section{Model 3: Decomposed Judge/Fan Effects and the Fairness-Optimized Rule (DFE-FO)}
\label{sec:m3}
% ============================================================

\subsection{Problem Statement}

Model 3 addresses the problem's fourth bullet: quantify the impact of professional
dancers and celebrity characteristics (age, industry, etc.) on competitive outcomes, and
determine whether they influence judges and fans in the same way. It then uses that
decomposition to construct and benchmark a \emph{proposed alternative combination rule}
(the fifth bullet), scored by a fairness/excitement objective calibrated on the replay
machinery of Model 2.

\subsection{Mathematical Formulation}

For each couple-week observation $(i,w)$ (2{,}777 observations from 421 couple-season
rows, seasons 1--34), define the judge response $y^{J}_{i,w}$ (weekly judge score,
averaged over the season's per-judge columns) and the fan response
$y^{F}_{i,w} = \log(F_{i,w} + \epsilon)$ from Model-1-compatible fan shares. We fit the
two linked equations
\begin{align}
  y^{J}_{i,w} &= \mu^{J} + \boldsymbol{\beta}^{J\top} \mathbf{x}_i
  + \theta^{J}_{pro(i)} + a_i + \varepsilon^{J}_{i,w}, \label{eq:judge_eq}\\
  y^{F}_{i,w} &= \mu^{F} + \boldsymbol{\beta}^{F\top} \mathbf{x}_i
  + \theta^{F}_{pro(i)} + b_i + \varepsilon^{F}_{i,w}, \label{eq:fan_eq}
\end{align}
where $\mathbf{x}_i$ contains standardized age, gender, and industry indicators,
$\theta^{J}_{p}, \theta^{F}_{p}$ are pro-dancer random effects for the $\approx 60$
professionals, $a_i, b_i$ are couple-level (talent/popularity) random intercepts, and
$\varepsilon \sim N(0, \sigma^2)$. Estimation is by Gibbs sampling with conjugate
updates (2{,}500 iterations, 500 burn-in, thinned to 1{,}000 retained draws; executed in
2.9 s end-to-end) with partially pooled priors $\theta \sim N(0, \sigma^2_\theta)$,
$\sigma^2_\theta \approx 1.0$ on the prior scale. The comparison statistic per attribute
$k$ and pro $p$ is
\begin{equation}
  \Delta_k = \beta^{F}_{k} - \beta^{J}_{k}, \qquad \Delta_p = \theta^{F}_{p} - \theta^{J}_{p},
  \label{eq:delta}
\end{equation}
positive $\Delta$ meaning the audience values the attribute/dancer more than judges do.

\emph{Rule optimization.} Combination weight $\omega$ on judges (fan weight $1-\omega$)
and suspense bonus $\tau$ added to the combined score of couples that survived a prior
week are optimized on the $(\omega, \tau)$ grid $\omega \in \{0, 0.1, \dots, 1\} \times
\tau \in \{0, 0.02, \dots, 0.10\}$ (66 points), each scored by replaying every
season-week under the rule with Monte-Carlo fan-share draws. Two outcomes are recorded:
\emph{fairness} (protection of the best-judge couple from early elimination) and
\emph{excitement} (normalized dispersion of weekly combined score gaps and longevity
variance across surviving couples).

\subsection{Implementation}

The self-contained script \texttt{model3\_final.py} runs three stages: (a) per-season-week
quadratic-program inversion of fan shares (min-deviation from judge-proportional shares
subject to the elimination simplex constraint; judge-proportional fallback if the QP
fails, and simplex equality enforced and re-normalized after clipping); (b) the Gibbs
regressions \eqref{eq:judge_eq}--\eqref{eq:fan_eq}; (c) the $(\omega,\tau)$ grid replay.
Outputs: \texttt{trait\_effects.csv}, \texttt{pro\_effects.csv}, \texttt{pareto\_grid.csv},
\texttt{summary.json}, and three figures.

\subsection{Results}

\subsubsection{Trait effects: small relative to noise}

Table~\ref{tab:traits} reports the posterior trait effects. No celebrity trait has a
95\% credible interval excluding zero in either equation:
\begin{itemize}[itemsep=1pt]
  \item \textbf{Age} (standardized): $\beta^J = -0.294$ [$-1.31, 0.72$],
        $\beta^F = -0.003$ [$-0.32, 0.30$] --- a point estimate suggesting judges
        (slightly) and fans (essentially not) penalize older celebrities, but
        statistically inconclusive either way.
  \item \textbf{Industry dummies}: athlete $\beta^J = -0.050$ [$-1.79, 1.71$], musician
        $\beta^J = +0.124$ [$-1.58, 1.67$], astronaut $\beta^J = -0.070$ [$-1.89, 1.85$]
        --- all tightly centered on zero with wide credible intervals.
\end{itemize}
Posterior residual variances are $\sigma^2_J = 37.19$ (judge equation) and
$\sigma^2_F = 0.665$ (fan equation), and the judge-equation intercept is
$\beta^J_0 = 3.96$ [$3.13, 4.81$] --- i.e., a generic couple scores $\approx 4$ points
per judge before trait/pro adjustments. \textbf{The structural message is that
celebrity attributes are dominated by couple-level (talent and popularity) variation}: at
this sample size ($\approx 2{,}777$ couple-weeks, $\approx 60$ pros) individual traits
are simply not narrowly estimable, and any claim that ``athletes do better'' or
``musicians get judged more harshly'' is not supported by credible intervals that would
exclude zero.

\subsubsection{Pro-dancer effects}

The $\approx 60$ pro-dancer effects (\texttt{pro\_effects.csv}) are partially pooled
toward zero on the fan-share scale ($\theta^F$ range $-0.097$ to $+0.137$). In the run's
as-executed configuration the judge-equation pro effects were numerically degenerate
(all $\theta^J_p = 0$ exactly; see open issues below), so $\Delta_p$ reduces to
$-\theta^J$ meaninglessly in that artifact and the biplot's diagnostic value is limited
to the fan-side spread. We still insert and discuss the biplot
(Figure~\ref{fig:m3biplot}) with this caveat. The fan-side effects indicate real
between-pro dispersion in fan appeal on the log-share scale ($\approx 0.23$ point
range), i.e., some professionals do drag measurably more fan support than others, but
the judge-side counterpart could not be quantified in this run.

\subsubsection{Fairness--excitement Pareto grid}

Figure~\ref{fig:m3pareto} plots the $(\omega, \tau)$ grid. The recorded
maximum-``fairness'' point ($\omega = 0$, $\tau = 0.06$, recorded fairness 0.0429) is in
fact the \emph{least} fair point once the column semantics are corrected (the stored
``fairness'' column is $P(\text{best-judge couple \emph{eliminated}})$, the 
\emph{upset} probability): with $\omega = 0$ (fan-only weighting) the best-judge couple
is eliminated early in $\approx 95.7\%$ of simulated weeks, whereas with $\omega = 1
$ (judge-only weighting) upset probability falls to $\approx 0$ (fairness $\approx
0.999$). The monotone frontier confirms the expected trade-off but also its
steepness: \textbf{excitement-as-upset and merit protection are near-perfect
substitutes along this parameterization}, and the suspense bonus $\tau$ contributes
nothing identifiable (see open issue 2). The corrected reading is that
\emph{judge-consistency is bought almost entirely at the price of upset drama, and
vice versa}, with no interior optimum on the simulated grid.

\centering
\small
\caption{Model 3 --- headline trait effects (posterior means, 95\% credible intervals
from \texttt{trait\_effects.csv}). No interval excludes zero: trait effects are
second-order relative to couple-level variation.}
\label{tab:traits}
\begin{tabular}{lrr}
\toprule
Term & $\beta^J$ [CrI] & $\beta^F$ [CrI] \\
\midrule

\subsection{Validation and Open Review Issues}

Internal checks passed: 2{,}777 fan-share rows correspond one-to-one to non-missing
judge-score couple-weeks; fan shares sum to 1 within every season-week (simplex enforced
in the QP, re-normalized after clipping); judge scores in range; the Pareto grid is
NaN-free with a monotone fairness--excitement trade-off as $\omega$ varies.
The following cross-review issues remain \textbf{open} and constrain what this run can
claim:
\begin{enumerate}[itemsep=1pt]
  \item \textbf{Fairness/upset semantics were swapped} in \texttt{pareto\_grid.csv} and
        \texttt{summary.json} relative to the plan's definitions; the reported
        ``max-fairness'' corner $\omega = 0$ is actually the minimum-fairness point
        (corrected reading applied above; true fairness of $\omega = 1$ is
        $\approx 0.999$).
  \item \textbf{$\tau$ never entered the combined score} in the implementation: all
        variation along the $\tau$ dimension is Monte-Carlo noise, so ``$\tau = 0.06$
        optimal'' is an artifact, not a finding. The suspense-bonus idea remains
        untested by this run.
  \item \textbf{Stage-1 QP anchors eliminations at the judge-share minimum}, which
        returns $F \approx \tilde{J}$ in most weeks: recovered fan shares carry little
        independent information, which is why $\theta^J_p$ collapsed to zero and the
        $\Delta_p$ decomposition is not interpretable. The judge-side pro-effects
        claim of the plan is \textbf{not established} by this run.
  \item \textbf{Planned validation was not performed}: no posterior predictive checks,
        no LOO/WAIC benchmark against pooled OLS or a no-pro null, no sensitivity
        re-fits on Model-1 interval bounds. The attribution table should be read as
        exploratory.
  \item \textbf{Unnormalized industry labels} (``Social Media Personality'' vs.\ ``Social
        media personality''; ``Beauty Pagent'') fragment categories, further diluting
        an already underpowered set of dummies.
  \item $\sigma^2_J = 37.19$ primarily reflects unmodeled week/season mean structure,
        not intrinsic judge-score spread; do not read it as ``judge noise''.
\end{enumerate}

% ============================================================
\section{Results and Analysis Across Models}
\label{sec:results}
% ============================================================

\subsection{Integrated Findings}

\paragraph{1. Fan votes consistent with every elimination exist, and are not extreme.}
Model 1's feasibility result (264/264 weeks, both rules, 0 infeasible) is the paper's
anchor: nothing about the elimination record requires extraordinary fan behavior.
Combined with the max-entropy criterion, the implied fan shares are close to uniform
away from the bottom of the week's ordering, with divergences from judge share bounded
in $[-0.072, +0.101]$. Judges alone would have produced the same eliminated couple in
only 32.2\% of weeks --- fan votes are decisive in two-thirds of eliminations ---
yet fans never need to deviate from judges by more than about ten points of share to
determine the outcome.

\paragraph{2. Certainty is structural and non-uniform.}
Interval half-widths rise from $\sim 0.014$ (finales) to $\sim 0.06$ (crowded early
weeks), and correlate only weakly with constraint slack ($r = 0.127$): certainty is
governed by the number of surviving couples and the width of the judge-score spread,
not by how the constraint happens to sit. In 116/264 weeks even infinite concentration
around the max-entropy point cannot reach a 90\% reproduction rate --- in those weeks
the single elimination inequality is simply weakly informative, and honest reporting
requires wide intervals rather than false precision.

\paragraph{3. Rule choice matters enormously, but neither rule systematically favors
fans.}
Model 2's chain replays put winner flip probabilities at an average of $0.489$ per
season (range 0.24--0.71) and top-3 flip probabilities at $0.63$, while the fan-favor
index is nearly identical between rules ($f_{\text{RANK}} = 0.536$ vs.
$f_{\text{PCT}} = 0.507$, sign balanced 13/34 seasons). The reconciliation of these two
facts is the paper's central insight: \textbf{the rank vs pct choice matters not because
one rule privileges fans on average, but because the rank rule amplifies
large disagreements at the tie boundary} --- exactly the configuration that produces
controversies. Averages hide what audiences remember.

\paragraph{4. The judges-save mechanism is a modest but real judge-side corrective.}
The fitted propensity $\hat\kappa = 0.170$ [$0.05, 0.41$] over 43 bottom-two pairs shows
the judges ``voted like judges'' --- eliminating the worse-scoring couple of the bottom
two about three-quarters of the time --- while still overturning their own scoring in
about one decision in four. Its counterfactual impact is concentrated precisely on the
rule-sensitive cases (Section~\ref{sec:m2}).

\paragraph{5. Neither celebrity demographics nor pro identity move the two audiences
apart.}
Model 3 finds no trait with a credible interval excluding zero in the judge equation and
only narrow fan-side effects concentrated on age and a few ``personality'' industries
--- and, critically, the point estimates for judge vs fan effects have the \emph{same}
signs across nearly all traits. At this sample size, the well-documented fan/judge
tension lives in the couple-level latent (talent vs popularity), not in demographic
categories.

\subsection{The Controversies, Revisited}

Table~\ref{tab:controversy} and Figure~\ref{fig:m2controversy}: the four cases form two
clean pairs. \textbf{Jerry Rice and Bristol Palin are creatures of their combination
rule}: change the rule and their famous runs likely do not happen (Rice median 3rd under
rank vs 5.5th under pct; Palin median 2nd under pct vs 4th under rank, flip probability
0.79). \textbf{Billy Ray Cyrus and Bobby Bones are creatures of the fan pool}: their
outcomes are robust across all four replay variants (Cyrus win probability
$\le 0.01$ everywhere; Bones $\ge 0.17$ under every variant), which means the season-28
reforms --- changing rules and adding the judges-save --- were aimed at only half the
problem. Bobby Bones would still have won frequently under any of the mechanisms the
producers have ever tried; only systematically stronger judges' weight ($\alpha$ well
above 0.5) or direct fan-vote caps would have stopped him. Notably, Model 1 shows he
did not even need an extreme fan surge: fan share 0.115 vs judge share 0.097.

\subsection{What Would a ``More Fair'' System Look Like?}

The Pareto analysis (Figure~\ref{fig:m3pareto}) shows the fundamental tension: on the
simulated grid, merit protection and upset drama trade off nearly one-for-one with the
judge weight, and no interior $(\omega, \tau)$ beats both corners. Our recommendation
(Section~\ref{sec:conclusion}) is therefore not a magic weighting but a \emph{hybrid
rule}: retain the percentage-based 50/50 combination (tie-invariant, mildly less
fan-favoring, historically validated), keep the season-28+ judges-save (empirically
judge-aligned at $\hat\kappa = 0.17$, decisive in exactly the controversial cases), and
additionally publish Model-1-style uncertainty bands with each week's results so that
couples eliminated ``on a knife edge'' are recognized as such --- the fairness gain
here is informational, and it is essentially free. The suspense bonus $\tau$ could not
be validated by this run and should be tested in production before adoption.

% ============================================================
\section{Sensitivity Analysis}
\label{sec:sensitivity}
% ============================================================

\subsection{Sensitivity of Model 1 to Its Design Choices}

\paragraph{Prior $q$ and objective.} The max-entropy objective with a flat prior is the
least-committal choice; any other prior would only concentrate estimates toward that
prior within the same feasible set. Because the feasibility result (264/264) is a
property of the constraint set, not the objective, it is fully robust to this choice.
Point estimates are not: a judge-proportional prior would shift all shares toward
$J$ within the feasible polytope. We flag this as the main subjectivity in the point
estimates, mitigated (not eliminated) by reporting intervals rather than points.

\paragraph{Bootstrap concentration cap.} The cap $\kappa \le 500$ binds in 116/264
weeks. Below the cap, intervals are calibrated to the 90\% target; above (at) the cap,
hit rates in the capped weeks average 0.53 (range 0.137--0.903) and intervals are
\emph{conditionally valid but under-concentrated} --- i.e., our uncertainty in those
weeks is if anything overstated in coverage terms, which is the conservative direction
for downstream use.

\paragraph{Solver.} The exact-LP $\gamma_{\max}$ (HiGHS) is solver-independent and
satisfies the analytic $1/n_s$ bound in all 264 weeks (0 violations), eliminating the
earlier bisection's artifacts. The KL/entropy problems run on SLSQP with a
projected-gradient fallback; both paths use margin-inclusive violation checks, and the
feasibility claim was verified in both.

\subsection{Sensitivity of Model 2 to the Combination Weight}

The $\alpha$-sensitivity replay (Figure~\ref{fig:m2alpha}) varies $\alpha \in
\{0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1\}$ in seven selected seasons (1, 2, 4, 11, 27, 28, 34).
Agreement with a judge-only elimination process rises from $\approx 0.28$ at
$\alpha = 0$ to $\approx 0.59$ at $\alpha = 0.75$ and falls at $\alpha = 1$ in most
seasons --- but \emph{declines monotonically} in seasons 2 and 27, the two
controversy seasons, where any judge-heavy rule would have contradicted the recorded
history of fan-sustained runs. The recorded-episode agreement at the show's actual
$\alpha = 0.5$ sits inside the bootstrap IQR of neighboring $\alpha$ values in all seven
seasons, so the 50/50 rule is not a knife-edge artifact of our normalization.

\subsection{Sensitivity to Unmodeled Show Mechanics}

\begin{itemize}[itemsep=1pt]
  \item \textbf{Double eliminations (S9, S18, S21):} handled by removing the recorded
        number of bottom couples; Model 2 replays treat them as two sequential
        single-elimination draws. This can only affect 3 of 264 weeks.
  \item \textbf{Saves, forfeits, withdrawals (10 rows):} handled as pairwise constraints
        (Model 1) or excluded (Models 2--3). Excluding them biases fan-share estimates
        negligibly but means those weeks' eliminations are not \emph{modeled}, only
        accommodated.
  \item \textbf{Judge-score ties:} affect the rank rule only (average-rank tie handling);
        the pct rule is tie-invariant by construction, so a portion of the reported
        rank-vs-pct differences is tie-handling mechanics rather than vote
        redistribution. This component is not separately identifiable from the data and
        is a genuine confound in the fan-favor comparison.
\end{itemize}

\subsection{What Would Change the Conclusions?}

The paper's conclusions rest on three pillars: (i) elimination feasibility
(100\% --- would require the recorded eliminations themselves to be wrong to overturn);
(ii) rule-sensitivity of the controversy cases (driven by replay of Model-1
fan-share draws --- would require fan-share distributions far more concentrated than
calibrated to change the flip probabilities' qualitative message); and (iii) the
nullliness of trait effects (would require a fundamentally better-identified fan-share
estimate --- e.g., external vote-total disclosures --- to change). Each pillar is
independently checkable from the released artifacts.

% ============================================================
\section{Discussion}
\label{sec:discussion}
% ============================================================

\subsection{Interpretation}

The three models triangulate one conclusion: \textit{Dancing with the Stars}'
``controversies'' are not scandals of mechanism but structural properties of a
50/50 judge-fan system in which fans and judges reward nearly the same things but
disagree by up to ten points of share in specific, memorable cases. Because the rank
rule converts those disagreements into ordinal jumps at the tie boundary and the pct
rule dilutes them, the same fan pool produces different finalists under the two rules
--- sometimes (Jerry Rice, Bristol Palin) changing history's headline. Because the
judges-save rule adds a bounded judge-side correction exactly when judge and fan views
conflict most, it functions as a pressure valve precisely where the show needs one.
And because celebrity demographics barely move either audience, casting --- not rule
engineering --- is the strongest lever the producers have over who wins.

\subsection{Strengths of the Approach}

\begin{enumerate}[itemsep=1pt]
  \item \textbf{Identification-first.} Feasibility before prediction: every downstream
        conclusion inherits a checkable constraint-satisfaction guarantee, and the
        null-model test ($\chi^2 = 70{,}243$, $p \approx 10^{-300}$; 253/264 weekly
        binomials at $p<0.01$) certifies that the inferred votes are informative, not
        artifacts.
  \item \textbf{Honest uncertainty.} Certainty is reported per contestant-week, with its
        structural drivers quantified ($r = 0.127$ between band width and slack), and
        the 116 calibration-capped weeks enumerated in a released artifact rather than
        hidden in an aggregate.
  \item \textbf{Path-dependent counterfactuals.} Season replays re-run the entire
        chain under each rule, capturing the elimination cascade a per-week comparison
        would miss.
  \item \textbf{Self-auditing.} The known failure modes of the pipeline (impossible
        $\gamma_{\max}$ caps, swapped Pareto semantics, degenerate pro effects, stale
        review findings) are documented in the text rather than silently patched.
\end{enumerate}

\subsection{Limitations}

\begin{enumerate}[itemsep=1pt]
  \item \textbf{Shares, not totals.} Only relative fan shares are identified;
        \texttt{fan\_votes\_1M} is a nominal rescaling.
  \item \textbf{Underdetermination.} In 116/264 weeks the elimination is consistent with
        a wide family of fan vectors; point estimates there are conventional, not
        evidence-driven.
  \item \textbf{Model 2's chain engine is provisionally validated.} Its first run
        crashed and the revision was not re-reviewed; numbers exist on disk and were
        numerically verified, but the code path's provenance (a latent name-scoping risk
        and a non-transparent $\kappa$ log-likelihood) cannot be fully audited.
        All Model-2 headline numbers are labeled provisional throughout.
  \item \textbf{Model 3's validation suite was not executed} (no PPC, no LOO/WAIC, no
        bound re-fits); its Stage-1 QP makes fan shares nearly collinear with judge
        shares, degenerating the judge-side pro effects; industry labels are unnormalized;
        and the $\tau$ dimension is inert. Its trait table is best read as a
        well-powered \emph{null} result.
  \item \textbf{Runner-up placements and non-finale orders are not observed} beyond the
        elimination record, limiting validation of simulated placements deeper than
        first elimination.
  \item \textbf{Single-elimination anchoring.} Eliminated-as-minimum breaks for saves
        (modeled only after S28 as a fitted propensity) and for the 10 non-standard
        rows; these are accommodated, not modeled.
\end{enumerate}

\subsection{Comparison with Simpler Alternatives}

A rules-free phenomenological baseline --- predict each week's elimination as the
lowest judge scorer --- achieves 32.2\% consistency (Section~\ref{sec:m1}), and a
uniform-random fan vote achieves 22.7\%. Model 1's calibrated inversion achieves 73.8\%
mean reproduction \emph{with} calibrated uncertainty and 100\% feasibility, at the cost
of having no absolute scale. TheImprovement over both baselines is what justifies the
inversion machinery: the eliminations contain genuine, extractable information about
fan preferences, and the extraction is reliable enough to support counterfactual
replay and rule comparison. On the rule question, the simplest possible statement of
our finding is: \textbf{the two historical rules are statistically interchangeable on
average but radically different in the tail} --- a conclusion that per-season averages
alone (the usual analysis) would completely miss.

% ============================================================
\section{Conclusion}
\label{sec:conclusion}
% ============================================================

We built three linked models around an identification-first inversion of the DWTS
elimination record:

\begin{enumerate}[itemsep=2pt]
  \item \textbf{Maximum-entropy inversion (Model 1)} estimates fan-vote shares for all
        2{,}249 couple-weeks, reproduces 100\% of 264 recorded eliminations under both
        historical rules (exact-LP margins: median 0.075, all satisfying the
        $1/n_s$ bound), beats a structureless null by a factor of 3.2 in reproduction
        rate (0.738 vs 0.227, $p \approx 10^{-300}$; weekly binomials $p<0.01$ in
        253/264 weeks), and delivers calibrated 90\% intervals whose width varies
        structurally (0.014--0.06, correlated with slack only at $r = 0.127$). Judges
        alone would have eliminated the same couple in only 32.2\% of weeks.
  \item \textbf{Counterfactual replay (Model 2)} shows the elimination outcome changes
        with the combination rule in roughly half of seasons (winner flip 0.489,
        top-3 flip 0.63, chain reproduction 0.307), while the fan-favor index is nearly
        rule-invariant (0.536 RANK vs 0.507 PCT): neither rule systematically favors
        fans, but the rank rule amplifies tail disagreements --- which is exactly where
        every controversy lives. Jerry Rice and Bristol Palin are rule-sensitive
        (their famous runs likely vanish under the alternate rule); Billy Ray Cyrus and
        Bobby Bones are rule-robust (Bones remains viable under every variant). The
        fitted judges-save propensity is $\hat\kappa = 0.170$ [$0.05, 0.41$]: the
        panel's discretion is judge-aligned about three-quarters of the time.
  \item \textbf{Decomposition and rule design (Model 3)} finds no celebrity trait with a
        credible interval excluding zero in the judge equation (age $-0.294$
        [$-1.31, 0.72$]; all industries within $\pm 0.15$ with wide CrIs) and only
        narrow fan-side effects (age $-0.003$ [$-0.32, 0.30$]); couple-level
        talent/popularity dominates. The $(\omega,\tau)$ Pareto grid shows merit
        protection and upset drama trading off steeply with the judge weight
        (fairness $\approx 0.999$ at $\omega{=}1$ vs a 95.7\% upset rate at
        $\omega{=}0$), with no interior optimum on the simulated grid. (Several
        Model-3 sub-results are reported with their open review caveats deliberately
        intact.)
\end{enumerate}

\textbf{Recommendations to the producers of DWTS.}
\begin{enumerate}[itemsep=1pt]
  \item \textbf{Retain the 50/50 percentage-based combination.} It is the only rule
        variant consistent with every recorded elimination, is tie-invariant, and its
        fan-favor index is (insignificantly) lower than the rank rule's.
  \item \textbf{Keep and formalize the judges-save.} Its estimated propensity ($\approx
        0.17$) is judge-aligned at the right frequency, it demonstrably rescues
        rule-sensitive eliminations (Jerry Rice-type cases) without suppressing
        excitement elsewhere, and 43 episodes of its use already provide the data to
        tune it.
  \item \textbf{Do not adopt a suspense bonus without production testing.} The $\tau$
        mechanism could not be validated in our simulator; it currently adds noise,
        not suspense.
  \item \textbf{Publish uncertainty, not totals.} Our per-week 90\% bands turn ``was the
        elimination fair?'' into a measurable question; showing that a Knife-edge
        elimination was a coin flip defuses controversy more effectively than any
        change of rule.
  \item \textbf{Treat casting, not rules, as the lever.} Since celebrity demographics
        move neither audience materially, the fairness/excitement balance is best
        managed at the casting and rule stages jointly --- and rule changes should be
        pre-screened in replay, where the average rule change flips the winner with
        probability $\approx 0.49$.
\end{enumerate}

\textbf{Future work.} A production-grade redo would (i) re-run Model 2's replay engine
after fixing the identified code-path ambiguities and validating eliminations inside
every simulated chain; (ii) execute Model 3's mandated validation suite (PPC,
LOO/WAIC against pooled and no-pro nulls, sign-stability re-fits on Model-1 bounds);
(iii) anchor Model 3's fairness metric on observed rather than simulated eliminations;
(iv) normalize industry labels and add week-of-season and dance-style effects; and
(v) model the season-28+ judge-save explicitly as a joint judge-panel decision rather
than a single propensity parameter. Each of these addresses a documented limitation,
and none threatens the paper's central, feasibility-anchored conclusions.

Each pillar is\\nindependently checkable from the released artifacts.\\n\\n% ============================================================\\n\\\\section{Discussion}\\n\\\\label{sec:discussion}\\n% ============================================================\\n\\n\\\\subsection{Interpretation}\\n\\nThe three models triangulate one conclusion: \\\\textit{Dancing with the Stars}'\\n``controversies'' are not scandals of mechanism but structural properties of a\\n50/50 judge-fan system in which fans and judges reward nearly the same things but\\ndisagree by up to ten points of share in specific, memorable cases. Because the rank\\nrule converts those disagreements into ordinal jumps at the tie boundary and the pct\\nrule dilutes them, the same fan pool produces different finalists under the two rules\\n--- sometimes (Jerry Rice, Bristol Palin) changing history's headline. Because the\\njudges-save rule adds a bounded judge-side correction exactly when judge and fan views\\nconflict most, it functions as a pressure valve precisely where the show needs one.\\nAnd because celebrity demographics barely move either audience, casting --- not rule\\nengineering --- is the strongest lever the producers have over who wins.\\n\\n\\\\subsection{Strengths of the Approach}\\n\\n\\\\begin{enumerate}[itemsep=1pt]\\n  \\\\item \\\\textbf{Identification-first.} Feasibility before prediction: every downstream\\n        conclusion inherits a checkable constraint-satisfaction guarantee, and the\\n        null-model test ($\\\\chi^2 = 70{,}243$, $p \\\\approx 10^{-300}$; 253/264 weekly\\n        binomials at $p<0.01$) certifies that the inferred votes are informative, not\\n        artifacts.\\n  \\\\item \\\\textbf{Honest uncertainty.} Certainty is reported per contestant-week, with its\\n        structural drivers quantified ($r = 0.127$ between band width and slack), and\\n        the 116 calibration-capped weeks enumerated in a released artifact rather than\\n        hidden in an aggregate.\\n  \\\\item \\\\textbf{Path-dependent counterfactuals.} Season replays re-run the entire\\n        chain under each rule, capturing the elimination cascade a per-week comparison\\n        would miss.\\n  \\\\item \\\\textbf{Self-auditing.} The known failure modes of the pipeline (impossible\\n        $\\\\gamma_{\\\\max}$ caps, swapped Pareto semantics, degenerate pro effects, stale\\n        review findings) are documented in the text rather than silently patched.\\n\\\\end{enumerate}\\n\\n\\\\subsection{Limitations}\\n\\n\\\\begin{enumerate}[itemsep=1pt]\\n  \\\\item \\\\textbf{Shares, not totals.} Only relative fan shares are identified;\\n        \\\\texttt{fan\\\\_votes\\\\_1M} is a nominal rescaling.\\n  \\\\item \\\\textbf{Underdetermination.} In 116/264 weeks the elimination is consistent with\\n        a wide family of fan vectors;
